title: NHS: Periods
text: Periods are part of the menstrual cycle. The first day of a period is day one of the cycle. Period patterns vary. Seek medical advice if periods are very heavy, significantly painful, irregular in a concerning way, or if you are worried about a change.

title: MedlinePlus: Menstruation
text: The menstrual cycle includes changes that prepare the body for a possible pregnancy. Cycle length and bleeding can vary. Keeping track of period dates and symptoms can help you discuss patterns with a health professional.

title: U.S. Office on Women's Health: Your menstrual cycle
text: Period products include disposable pads and reusable cloth pads, as well as tampons, menstrual cups, and period underwear. Choose a product that feels comfortable and suits your flow. Change menstrual products regularly and follow the product's instructions. Wash reusable products according to their care instructions.

title: NHS: Heavy periods
text: Heavy periods can include needing to change a pad or tampon every one to two hours, bleeding for more than seven days, or bleeding through clothes or bedding. If heavy bleeding affects daily life, seek medical advice.

title: ACOG: Dysmenorrhea: Painful Periods
text: Period cramps are common, but severe pain or pain that disrupts daily activities deserves medical assessment. A clinician can help identify causes and discuss treatment options.

title: CDC: About menstrual hygiene
text: Good menstrual hygiene includes changing menstrual products regularly and washing hands before and after changing them. Follow product directions and keep reusable products clean. If a product causes irritation, stop using it and consider an unscented alternative.

title: NHS: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
text: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common condition that affects how the ovaries work. Its three main features are irregular periods (the ovaries may not regularly release eggs), higher levels of androgens (sometimes called 'male' hormones), which can cause signs such as excess facial or body hair, oily skin or acne, and polycystic ovaries, where the ovaries become enlarged and contain many fluid-filled sacs (follicles). Other signs can include weight gain, thinning hair on the head and difficulty getting pregnant. The exact cause is not known, but it often runs in families and is linked to higher insulin levels. There is no cure, but symptoms can be managed with lifestyle changes such as a healthy weight and diet, and with medicines. See a GP if you have symptoms or are worried you might have PCOS.

title: MedlinePlus: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
text: PCOS is a hormone imbalance that can cause irregular or missed periods and is a common cause of infertility. People with PCOS have a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and heart problems. Diagnosis is based on a medical history, physical exam, blood tests to check hormone levels, and sometimes an ultrasound of the ovaries. Treatment depends on symptoms and goals and can include lifestyle changes, hormonal birth control to regulate periods, and other medicines.

title: NHS: Endometriosis
text: Endometriosis is a condition where tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows in other places, such as the ovaries and fallopian tubes. Symptoms can include pelvic pain, period pain that stops you doing normal activities, pain during or after sex, pain when peeing or pooing during a period, feeling sick, constipation or diarrhoea, and difficulty getting pregnant. Some people have no symptoms. It can take time to diagnose. Treatments include painkillers, hormone medicines and sometimes surgery. See a GP if you have symptoms of endometriosis, especially if they are having a big impact on your life.

title: NHS: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS)
text: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) is the name for symptoms some people get in the weeks before their period, such as mood swings, feeling upset, anxious or irritable, tiredness, trouble sleeping, bloating, breast tenderness, headaches, spotty skin and changes in appetite. Symptoms usually improve once the period starts. Regular exercise, a healthy diet, enough sleep, and reducing stress may help, and keeping a symptom diary can help you and a GP see patterns. A severe form called premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) can seriously affect mood; see a GP if symptoms are severe or affect daily life.

title: NHS: Stopped or missed periods
text: Periods can stop or be missed for many reasons. Common causes include pregnancy, stress, sudden weight loss, being overweight, doing too much exercise, taking some types of contraception, the menopause, and conditions such as PCOS. If you might be pregnant, take a pregnancy test. See a GP if you have missed more than 3 periods in a row and are not pregnant, if you are under 45 and your periods have stopped, or if you are worried.

title: NHS: Irregular periods
text: A normal menstrual cycle is often between 21 and 35 days, and it is common for cycle length to vary a little. Periods are often irregular in the first few years after they start and when approaching menopause. Irregular periods can also be caused by stress, weight changes, hormonal contraception and conditions such as PCOS or thyroid problems. See a GP if your periods suddenly become irregular, if your cycle is shorter than 21 days or longer than 35 days, or if you are worried.

title: NHS: Period pain
text: Period pain is common and usually felt as cramps in the tummy, which can spread to the back and thighs. Things that can help include painkillers such as ibuprofen or paracetamol (follow the packet instructions and check they are suitable for you), putting a heat pad or hot water bottle on your tummy, a warm bath, gentle exercise, and relaxation. See a GP if the pain is severe, has changed or got worse, or if you also have heavy bleeding, bleeding between periods or pain during sex, as these can be signs of conditions such as endometriosis.

title: NHS: Toxic shock syndrome
text: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a rare but life-threatening condition caused by bacteria getting into the body and releasing toxins. It is often linked to tampon use but can affect anyone. Symptoms can include a high temperature, flu-like symptoms, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, a widespread sunburn-like rash, dizziness or fainting, and confusion. Get urgent medical help if you have these symptoms, especially if you use tampons or a menstrual cup, and remove the tampon. To lower the risk, use the lowest absorbency tampon for your flow, change tampons as often as directed, and wash hands before and after inserting.
